sections.title: How does the Partial pressure calculator work?
sections.html:
The Partial pressure calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports henry's law constant (Henry's law - method 2) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the gas (Henry's law - method 1) and the gas (Henry's law - method 2)); then you type in the mole fraction (Dalton's law), the partial pressure (Dalton's law), amount of moles and the volume.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Partial pressure calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Henry's law constant=(1 ÷ 101325) × partial pressure ÷ mole fraction
Concentration=(1 ÷ 101325) × partial pressure ÷ henry's law constant
Temperature=(1 ÷ 4157231309076620) × (-1135547732074278753 × amount of moles + 500000000000000 × partial pressure × volume) ÷ amount of moles
Total pressure=partial pressure ÷ mole fraction

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Molar concentration, opening in molars
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Pressure, opening in standard atmospheres

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Partial pressure calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the mole fraction and the partial pressure — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Partial pressure calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns henry's law constant (Henry's law - method 2), derived from the mole fraction and the partial pressure. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Partial pressure calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the mole fraction and the partial pressure, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter total pressure in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Total pressure opens in kilopascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Henry's law constant = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Partial pressure calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
